Question: How does the platform enforce data residency dynamically at runtime for: model inference, tool calls, memory/state storage, logging? Is enforcement automatic, not developer-configured?
Response: Data residency is enforced at the platform level — automatic, not developer-configured. Enforcement mechanism: workflow state carries jurisdiction metadata (set when the workflow is created based on the hire location or invoice entity). APIM AI Gateway reads the jurisdiction and enforces routing: (1) Model inference — APIM routes to region-appropriate model endpoints. A workflow with jurisdiction=DE routes exclusively to EU-hosted model endpoints. Candidate PII from a German hire cannot reach US-hosted endpoints. (2) Tool calls — MCP tool calls route through APIM which enforces regional constraints. (3) State storage — Cosmos DB multi-region deployment with data residency controls. Workflow state for German hires stored in EU region. (4) Logging — OTEL telemetry and audit logs stored in region-appropriate Azure Log Analytics workspace. The developer writes no jurisdiction logic — they build skills and tools. The platform (APIM policies, Cosmos DB regions, Log Analytics workspaces) enforces residency based on workflow metadata. Runtime isolation backs residency enforcement: APIM is sole public edge in Private Endpoint mode; all backends (Cosmos, Key Vault, AI Search, Log Analytics, Event Grid, Foundry model endpoints) sit behind Private Endpoints — data never transits the public internet; Azure Functions runs VNet-integrated; Foundry Hosted Agents are in dedicated subnets with no public IPs; outbound SaaS traffic is restricted by Azure Firewall Premium FQDN allow-list. Region-pinned per jurisdiction — EU workflows never resolve US-region endpoints.
Key Technologies: APIM AI Gateway (jurisdiction routing), Cosmos DB (regional data residency), Azure Log Analytics (regional logging), workflow jurisdiction metadata

Question: Are deployment pipelines enforced with regional compliance checks before agents go live in a market? Are gates policy-driven, not manual checklists?
Response: Yes. Regional governance gates are policy-driven in the CI/CD pipeline. (1) API Center lifecycle: when a skill is promoted to Production for a specific market, the promotion gate validates compliance requirements for that market — does the skill include the required jurisdiction-specific compliance rules? Are the declared MCP tools available in the target region? Is the model deployment available in the target region? **API Center blocks the deployment if regional requirements are not met** — the skill cannot reach Production in the target market until all regional gates pass. (2) APIOps CI/CD: APIM policy deployment includes regional validation — policies are tested against regional compliance rules before deployment. (3) Foundry Guardrails: per-agent, per-region guardrail configuration. A guardrail set for EU markets enforces GDPR consent checks and PII handling rules. The guardrail configuration must be valid before the agent goes live. All gates are automated policy checks in the CI/CD pipeline, not manual checklists. Gate failures block deployment with specific compliance deficiency details. APIOps CI gate explicitly rejects PRs that register cross-region backends against jurisdiction-tagged skills (e.g. a DE-tagged skill cannot point to a US model endpoint or MCP backend); it also validates regional MCP tool availability, compliant model deployment in the target region, inclusion of required jurisdiction-specific compliance skills (GDPR consent, works council notifications for DE; right-to-work for UK; etc.), and alignment with the non-revocable operations catalogue.
Key Technologies: Azure API Center lifecycle gates, APIOps CI/CD, Foundry Guardrails (per-region), automated compliance validation
POC Demo: POC2: Show deployment gate — skill for German market validated against EU compliance requirements. Gate blocks if GDPR consent skill is not included.

Question: Describe continuous monitoring that agents behave within jurisdictional rules: detecting data crossing sovereignty boundaries, model endpoint region changes, non-compliant intermediaries.
Response: Runtime compliance monitoring operates continuously at three layers. (1) APIM AI Gateway: monitors all model and tool call routing. Detects if a request is routed to an endpoint outside the permitted region for its jurisdiction. Alerts on any sovereignty boundary crossing. Logs every routing decision for audit. (2) Foundry Guardrails: Task Adherence monitoring detects if an agent drifts from its jurisdiction-specific system message (e.g. a German hire workflow starts ignoring works council requirements). PII detection catches sensitive data in outputs regardless of jurisdiction. (3) Fleet Manager: continuously monitors compliance enforcement events from Foundry Guardrails and APIM. Detects patterns — repeated near-misses, jurisdiction switches that weren't caught, non-compliant intermediary services. Alerts surface on the Control Plane with severity level and recommended action. Microsoft Sentinel provides security-focused monitoring for sovereignty violations as part of broader threat detection.
Key Technologies: APIM (routing monitoring), Foundry Guardrails (Task Adherence), Fleet Manager (compliance pattern analysis), Microsoft Sentinel

Question: Can agents adapt behaviour based on jurisdiction (consent, retention, disclosure)? Is configuration declarative per jurisdiction, not hardcoded per agent?
Response: Yes. Jurisdiction-aware behaviour is declarative, not hardcoded. The mechanism: jurisdiction-specific skills. Each jurisdiction (USA, Germany, UK, etc.) has its own set of compliance skills that encode the local rules: (1) Germany: works council notification (BetrVG), GDPR consent management, employee data retention rules, EU AI Act conformity for automated screening. (2) USA: at-will employment rules, different consent requirements, no works council. (3) UK: right-to-work checks, UK GDPR, different data retention. When a workflow is created with a jurisdiction, the corresponding skills load automatically — MAF workflow graphs for that phase route to jurisdiction-specific validator and agent executor nodes that load the appropriate compliance skills. The agent developer writes the core workflow once. Jurisdiction-specific behaviour is layered on via declarative skills. Adding a new jurisdiction means adding new skill files, not modifying agent code. Data classification per jurisdiction: German hires encode works council notification (BetrVG), GDPR consent (Art. 6), data retention (3 years), EU AI Act conformity (documented bias assessment, mandatory HITL, transparency obligations). Non-revocable ops per jurisdiction (e.g. German hire = ServiceNow JML ticket for works council, Workday master data write) are Git-committed as jurisdiction skill variants and subject to dual-control where applicable. Skills are Git-versioned and managed through API Center lifecycle.
Key Technologies: Jurisdiction-specific SKILL.md files, Microsoft Agent Framework (MAF) workflow graphs (jurisdiction-specific executor routing), workflow jurisdiction metadata, API Center (skill management), Git version control
POC Demo: POC2 Appendix B: Show identical workflow for USA vs Germany — same core skills, different jurisdiction skills loaded automatically. Works council notification appears only for Germany.

Question: For high-risk agents: describe conformity assessment support, mandatory human oversight, transparency obligations, and technical documentation generation. Is risk classification integrated into the agent registry?
Response: EU AI Act compliance is addressed across the architecture. (1) Risk classification: skills and agents are classified by risk level in Azure API Center. High-risk classification (e.g. automated candidate screening) triggers additional governance requirements. Agent 365 (preview today, GA May 2026) correlates signals across Entra ID Protection, Defender, and Purview to assess agent risk. (2) Conformity assessment: the API Center lifecycle includes compliance validation gates. High-risk skills require additional review, testing, and documentation before Production promotion. Foundry Evaluators provide quality and bias assessments as part of conformity evidence. (3) Mandatory human oversight: HITL gates are enforced structurally at two points — GHCP SDK hooks inside the agent executor session, and MAF validator executor nodes between the agent executor and any action executor in the workflow graph. Judge/executor separation is an explicit node and edge, not a prompt. Autonomy thresholds for high-risk tasks default to maximum human oversight. The Control Plane provides the human oversight surface. (4) Transparency obligations: all automated screening decisions carry transparency markings (AI-generated, criteria used, human can override) AND cite the Foundry IQ knowledge sources that informed the decision (employment-law corpus version, policy document references, precedent cases). Candidates are informed of AI involvement per EU AI Act requirements and can be provided the cited sources on request. (5) Technical documentation: OTEL traces, skill definitions, model metadata, evaluation results, and governance policies collectively form the technical documentation package. Exportable from Foundry and Application Insights for regulatory submission. Reasoning chain is stored separately from the action ledger — a non-revocable action's audit entry carries the span ID that produced it, not the model's reasoning tokens, so auditors trace cause-and-effect without reasoning content becoming the audit record. No prompt/response bodies in App Insights (stored only in Log Analytics with Guardrails redaction). Platform certifications inherited from Azure — SOC 1/2 Type II/3, ISO 27001/27017/27018/27701, HIPAA, PCI DSS L1, FedRAMP High, GDPR, BSI C5 (Germany), EU AI Act alignment via Responsible AI Standard — provide the underlying compliance posture for conformity assessment evidence.
Key Technologies: API Center (risk classification), Foundry Evaluators (conformity evidence), GHCP SDK hooks + Microsoft Agent Framework (MAF) validator executors (mandatory HITL, judge/executor separation), transparency markings, OTEL documentation
